lesson.child_mission: Natural structures (termite mounds, spider webs, honeycomb) and built structures (houses, towers) both solve support and shelter problems with different materials.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same science idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Compare a tree and a wooden pole building: materials, who/what made it, purpose.

FEEDBACK
Tree grows/natural support and habitat; pole building is human-built for shelter — purposes may overlap (shade/shelter).

WATCH FOR
Thinking natural structures are “not real engineering” ignores how effective their shapes are.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Make a Venn diagram: natural structures / both / built structures with six examples. Write two shared purposes across the diagram.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Natural structures (termite mounds, spider webs, honeycomb) and built structures (houses, towers) both solve support and shelter problems with different materials.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Make a Venn diagram: natural structures / both / built structures with six examples. Write two shared purposes across the diagram. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Tree grows/natural support and habitat; pole building is human-built for shelter — purposes may overlap (shade/shelter). Reasoning: I used natural by attending to built and explain why it matters rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Thinking natural structures are “not real engineering” ignores how effective their shapes are. Correction: Tree grows/natural support and habitat; pole building is human-built for shelter — purposes may overlap (shade/shelter). Why: the correction restores accurate use of natural.

Parent: Likely misconception: Thinking natural structures are “not real engineering” ignores how effective their shapes are. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Investigate or describe a fresh example (not the worked objects) that uses natural. Record evidence and explain how it supports your claim.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about natural, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

Parent: Marking notes: Require a new example, named observations and a claim–evidence link. / Require misconception + corrected claim + evidence reason..

teach_steps.explain:
Natural structures (termite mounds, spider webs, honeycomb) and built structures (houses, towers) both solve support and shelter problems with different materials.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Thinking natural structures are “not real engineering” ignores how effective their shapes are. Correct the claim or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
